messages.subject: WAIC for censored survival models/data
parts:
Hi,
I have been fitting some censored survival data to various survival functions, in the below example to the siler distribution and trying to obtain WAIC scores for various different models. I have got it working on uncensored data but as soon as I have some censoring the WAIC seems to fail... all models have identical values. I have tried adjusting the control of the WAIC by using marginalizeNodes argument and also tried calculating it retrospectively with the posterior samples but cant seem to get it working? Am I missing something really obvious or is it just not possible in this type of model?!

I can provide full code if need be but I feel it must be something to do with the censored models I am trying to run as I had it working on the uncensored?

Many thanks
Dave

code <- nimbleCode({
 
  ## survival components
  for (i in 1:nind) {
   
    ## likelihood for interval-truncated Siler
    censored[i] ~ dinterval(tD[i], cint[i, ])
    tD[i] ~ dsilerNim(a1, a2, b1, b2, c1)
   
  }
 
  ## priors
  a1 ~ dexp(1)
  a2 ~ dexp(1)
  b1 ~ dexp(1)
  b2 ~ dexp(1)
  c1 ~ dexp(1)
 
})

messages.subject: Re: WAIC for censored survival models/data
parts:
Hi Chris,

Thank you!  Please see below for reproducable code.... it first simulates some 'death' times from the expoential distribution, then formats it ready for the model and then fits in NIMBLE... the WAIC I get matches exactly other models that I fit (for example with the custom distribution that I used above) and the pWAIC is always 0?

Any advice very gratefully received!

Many thanks
Dave

R code for WAIC comparisons:

library(tidyverse)
library(nimble)

## set up right censored data Exponential distributed data
## set parameters
r <- 0.005
censorRate <- 0.1
nind <- 500

## create sims
sims <- rexp(nind, r = r)

## censor results (1 = interval, 2 = right)
censored <- rbinom(length(sims), 1, censorRate) + 1

## adjust death times to make interval censored
sims <- ceiling(sims)

## adjust sims with random right-censored time
adjust <- which(censored == 2)
sims[adjust] <- sapply(sims[adjust], function(x) {
  sample(1:x, 1)
})

## setup data
tD <- rep(NA, length(sims))
tL <- sims - 1
tU <- sims

## define censoring matrices
## (here tL is lower bound and tU upper bound
## and sims is censoring time for right-censored
## so no further adjustments needed)
cint <- cbind(tL, tU)
colnames(cint) <- NULL
cint[censored == 2, 1] <- 0

## set up zL/zU input matrix
zL <- tL
zL[censored == 2] <- tU[censored == 2]

zU <- tU
zU[censored == 2] <- NA

## set maximum observation time
tM <- rep(ceiling(max(sims) + 1), length(sims))

##########################################################
##                                                      ##
## Now fit exponential model back to the data in NIMBLE ##
##                                                      ##
##########################################################

code <- nimbleCode({
  ## survival components for dead badgers
for (i in 1:nind) {
## likelihood for interval-truncated exponential
censored[i] ~ dinterval(tD[i], cint[i, ])

tD[i] ~ dexp(r)
  }
 
  ## priors
  r ~ dexp(1)
})

## set up other components of model
consts <- list(nind = nind)
data <- list(cint = cint, censored = censored, tD = tD)

## find overdispersed initial values
tinitFn <- function(cint, censored) {
  apply(cbind(cint, censored), 1, function(x) {
    if(x[3] == 2) {
      y <- x[2] + 1
    } else {
      y <- runif(1, x[1], x[2])
    }
    y
  })
}
initFn <- function(cint, censored) {
  ## get ML estimates as initial values
  optFn <- function(pars, t) {
    if(any(pars < 0)) {
      return(NA)
    }
    sum(dexp(t, r = pars[1], log = TRUE))
  }
  pars <- list(convergence = 1)
  k <- 0
  while(pars$convergence != 0 & k < 20) {
    ## sample missing values
    tD <- tinitFn(cint, censored)
    pars <- optim(rexp(1, 100), optFn, t = tD, control = list(fnscale = -1))
    k <- k + 1
  }
  if(k == 20) {
    stop("Can't sample initial values")
  }
  pars <- pars$par
  list(
    tD = tD,
    r = pars[1]
  )
}

## define the model, data, inits and constants
model <- nimbleModel(code = code, constants = consts, data = data, inits = initFn(cint, censored))

## compile the model
cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

## set monitor
config <- configureMCMC(cmodel, monitors = c("r"), thin = 1, enableWAIC = TRUE)

## check monitors and samplers
config$printMonitors()
config$printSamplers("r")

## build the model
built <- buildMCMC(config)
cbuilt <- compileNimble(built)

## run the model
system.time(run <- runMCMC(cbuilt,
                           niter = 20000,
                           nburnin = 5000,
                           nchains = 2,
                           progressBar = TRUE,
                           summary = TRUE,
                           samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,
                           thin = 1,
                           WAIC = TRUE))

## check samples
plot(run$samples)

## check WAIC
run$WAIC

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: WAIC for censored survival models/data
parts:
Hi Dave,

I don't believe WAIC makes sense here. You don't have any data (i.e., all of your tD values are missing). So the only contribution to the likelihood in the model is from "data$censored", but each of these always gives a likelihood contribution of 1 (a log-likelihood contribution of 0) because (based on the model construction, using dinterval) only values of tD that satisfy the censoring constraints are sampled. WAIC is calculated based on the density of the observations given the values of the sampled parameters at each iteration. In this case that is the density of the "censored" elements given the sampled "tD" elements.

If you want to use WAIC here, I think you need at least some of the tD values to be observed to be specific values.

-chris

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: WAIC for censored survival models/data
parts:
Hi Dave,

Perhaps what you want is a model that gives the probability of observing a given observation, which in your case is the probability of observing that the value is in an interval since you don't know the value exactly. That probability would be the integral over the known censoring interval of some distribution that represents the potential value of the observation, which you could hopefully compute in closed form. I.e., that distribution would be the distribution you would use for the likelihood in the situation where you imagine you could actually know the exact value of the observation (in your model code you are using an exponential). So if you could code up models specified in that way, I think you could use WAIC to compare such models. 

-chris
On Tue, Jan 11, 2022 at 11:06 PM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:

Hi Chris, 

Thanks for the explanation... my data comes is simulated to represent capture mark recapture data and I am modelling death times so the data I have will only give some boundaries to this. So I may have right censored death time (I only know that it is after a particular time point) or is interval censored (I know that it is after some point but before another). 

Would it be possible to use the boundaries in the calculation?

Many thanks

Dave

On Wednesday, 12 January 2022 at 01:29:14 UTC christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Dave,

I don't believe WAIC makes sense here. You don't have any data (i.e., all of your tD values are missing). So the only contribution to the likelihood in the model is from "data$censored", but each of these always gives a likelihood contribution of 1 (a log-likelihood contribution of 0) because (based on the model construction, using dinterval) only values of tD that satisfy the censoring constraints are sampled. WAIC is calculated based on the density of the observations given the values of the sampled parameters at each iteration. In this case that is the density of the "censored" elements given the sampled "tD" elements.

If you want to use WAIC here, I think you need at least some of the tD values to be observed to be specific values.

-chris

On Sun, Jan 9, 2022 at 11:29 PM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:
Hi Chris,

Thank you!  Please see below for reproducable code.... it first simulates some 'death' times from the expoential distribution, then formats it ready for the model and then fits in NIMBLE... the WAIC I get matches exactly other models that I fit (for example with the custom distribution that I used above) and the pWAIC is always 0?

Any advice very gratefully received!

Many thanks
Dave

R code for WAIC comparisons:

library(tidyverse)
library(nimble)

## set up right censored data Exponential distributed data
## set parameters
r <- 0.005
censorRate <- 0.1
nind <- 500

## create sims
sims <- rexp(nind, r = r)

## censor results (1 = interval, 2 = right)
censored <- rbinom(length(sims), 1, censorRate) + 1

## adjust death times to make interval censored
sims <- ceiling(sims)

## adjust sims with random right-censored time
adjust <- which(censored == 2)
sims[adjust] <- sapply(sims[adjust], function(x) {
  sample(1:x, 1)
})

## setup data
tD <- rep(NA, length(sims))
tL <- sims - 1
tU <- sims

## define censoring matrices
## (here tL is lower bound and tU upper bound
## and sims is censoring time for right-censored
## so no further adjustments needed)
cint <- cbind(tL, tU)
colnames(cint) <- NULL
cint[censored == 2, 1] <- 0

## set up zL/zU input matrix
zL <- tL
zL[censored == 2] <- tU[censored == 2]

zU <- tU
zU[censored == 2] <- NA

## set maximum observation time
tM <- rep(ceiling(max(sims) + 1), length(sims))

##########################################################
##                                                      ##
## Now fit exponential model back to the data in NIMBLE ##
##                                                      ##
##########################################################

code <- nimbleCode({
  ## survival components for dead badgers
  for (i in 1:nind) {
    ## likelihood for interval-truncated exponential
    censored[i] ~ dinterval(tD[i], cint[i, ])
    tD[i] ~ dexp(r)
  }
 
  ## priors
  r ~ dexp(1)
})

## set up other components of model
consts <- list(nind = nind)
data <- list(cint = cint, censored = censored, tD = tD)

## find overdispersed initial values
tinitFn <- function(cint, censored) {
  apply(cbind(cint, censored), 1, function(x) {
    if(x[3] == 2) {
      y <- x[2] + 1
    } else {
      y <- runif(1, x[1], x[2])
    }
    y
  })
}
initFn <- function(cint, censored) {
  ## get ML estimates as initial values
  optFn <- function(pars, t) {
    if(any(pars < 0)) {
      return(NA)
    }
    sum(dexp(t, r = pars[1], log = TRUE))
  }
  pars <- list(convergence = 1)
  k <- 0
  while(pars$convergence != 0 & k < 20) {
    ## sample missing values
    tD <- tinitFn(cint, censored)
    pars <- optim(rexp(1, 100), optFn, t = tD, control = list(fnscale = -1))
    k <- k + 1
  }
  if(k == 20) {
    stop("Can't sample initial values")
  }
  pars <- pars$par
  list(
    tD = tD,
    r = pars[1]
  )
}

## define the model, data, inits and constants
model <- nimbleModel(code = code, constants = consts, data = data, inits = initFn(cint, censored))

## compile the model
cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

## set monitor
config <- configureMCMC(cmodel, monitors = c("r"), thin = 1, enableWAIC = TRUE)

## check monitors and samplers
config$printMonitors()
config$printSamplers("r")

## build the model
built <- buildMCMC(config)
cbuilt <- compileNimble(built)

## run the model
system.time(run <- runMCMC(cbuilt,
                           niter = 20000,
                           nburnin = 5000,
                           nchains = 2,
                           progressBar = TRUE,
                           summary = TRUE,
                           samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,
                           thin = 1,
                           WAIC = TRUE))

## check samples
plot(run$samples)

## check WAIC
run$WAIC
